title: How To Teach While Wearing A Mask
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that masks strip away the facial cues and nonverbal communication teachers normally rely on, so effective mask-era teaching requires doubling down on three existing SCM strategies rather than inventing new ones. First, talk less: since most teachers already over-explain, cutting talking time by half or more becomes essential once a mask muffles speech. Second, model everything: silent, physical demonstration of routines and academic tasks replaces verbal explanation as the primary teaching tool. Third, focus on independence: giving students detailed models to work from, then releasing them to work while the teacher observes from a distance, reduces the reliance on real-time verbal communication altogether. He frames these three as pre-existing good practice that has now become essential rather than optional.
points: Masks remove facial cues students rely on, making excessive teacher talking especially costly.
Cut talking time by half to two-thirds; rely on brevity rather than explanation.
Replace verbal explanation with silent modeling of both routines and academic instruction wherever possible.
Use student modeling — having individuals or groups mimic actions — as a check for understanding.
Emphasize independent work so students can demonstrate mastery without relying on real-time verbal communication.
quotes: After all, students need to see your mouth and facial expressions to fully grasp your meaning.
In normal circumstances, most teachers talk way too much. They over-explain and digress off topic.
Even if you’re not prone to excessive talking, the less you speak while wearing a mask the better off you’ll be. Try cutting your talking by half or even two-thirds.
Instead of talking, model everything —at least until your students can perform the same repeatable actions all on their own.
The key is to show them in exacting detail what they need to do or know to succeed all on their own before turning them loose.
Talk less, model everything, and focus on independence. It was good teaching before the pandemic. Now, it’s essential.
